prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental realization of topologically protected edge transport in the quantum spin Hall and quantum anomalous Hall states, establishing topological insulators as a new class of quantum matter

statement.case_for: After reading all eight first-round statements I keep B003 as my preferred configuration, though by a narrower margin than at opening. The physics is the point. Kane's Z2 invariant showed that band topology, not symmetry breaking, can define a phase. Molenkamp's group then measured the predicted edge channels in HgTe wells as quantized conductance, and Xue's group measured quantized Hall resistance at zero field in magnetic topological insulator films. Each step is a quantitative result that has been checked against ARPES spectra and DFT band inversions, and it has been reproduced across HgTe, Bi-based and magnetically doped materials for more than fifteen years. That is the kind of verified, reproducible discovery I weigh most. To answer the chair's question directly: I treat QSH and QAH as one achievement, namely the experimental demonstration that a bulk-insulating material carries protected, dissipationless edge transport, first through spin-orbit physics and then through magnetism. They are two experiments, but they answer the same scientific question, and I would write the citation so that it says so. My preferred cut is Kane, Molenkamp and Xue. I would not go to Kane and Molenkamp alone, because dropping Xue removes the only demonstration that the topology survives without a magnetic field.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and I have not talked myself out of it. Mele is the co-author of the original Kane-Mele papers, Hasan's ARPES work established the three-dimensional materials, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal is what pointed Molenkamp at HgTe, with Zhang deceased. Three names cannot carry all of that, and the B018 cut fixes some of it only by dropping Xue and adding a fourth name. The 2016 prize also covers neighbouring ground, though I still think a model-system prize on topological phase transitions is different from one for real materials with protected edge states. Finally, a reader may see a bundle of two separate experiments. Against all this, B015 has an unusually clean attribution and the broadest support on the committee, and I have to ask whether a configuration that needs this much explanation of who is left out is really the better choice.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B014 to B015 after reading the other ballots. He asks whether QSH and QAH are one achievement or two, says he cannot judge this as a non-specialist, and wants B003 debated against B018 if it is to be considered.
responses.response: I will give you my answer as the member closest to this field. I read them as one achievement, namely protected edge transport in a bulk insulator, realized first with spin-orbit coupling and then with magnetism, and I would draft the citation that way. That is why I keep Xue. If the committee does not accept that reading, then B003 loses its third name and its argument, and I would not defend it against B015. Between B003 and B018, I still prefer B003, because B018 gains Mele and Hasan but gives up the only zero-field quantized-transport experiment. I also accept your point about wording: whatever we choose should name the specific discovery and not just a field.

responses.point: Danielsson agrees on the maturity and the theory-experiment pairing in B003 but objects that B003 and B018 split the same history, that Mele and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal are left out, and that he would not merge QAH with QSH just to fit three names.
responses.response: Your objection is fair and I think it is the strongest one against my ballot. I do not claim the three-name cut is obviously right. Where I disagree is on merging: the common thread is protected edge conduction in an insulator, and the QAH experiment is its decisive zero-field form, not a different subject. Your own concern with the credit is the reason I called Kane and Molenkamp the minimal fallback. I would not accept Hasan in place of Xue, since the 3D photoemission work largely confirms Fu-Kane-Mele predictions. On B014 I defer to you on the detector, but I agree with Pearce that the credit to two names from IceCube is the hard part, and I would not use that to push B003 ahead of it.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first and says its case is one of invention and measurement rather than surprise, that a citation must not imply lattice clocks alone define timekeeping, and that she has not independently verified priority between Katori, Lemonde and others.
responses.response: I take your candour about B015 as a mark of its quality, and it is the main reason I now rate it close to B003. As a theorist who values quantitative, reproduced results, I find the systematics budgets and the agreement between independent clocks as persuasive as anything on the list, and I have no physics objection. My remaining difference is kind: a new quantum phase that overturned what we thought bands could do is, to me, a bigger step than a better clock. I agree with your wording point, and if the committee goes with B015 I would want the citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice clock and not timekeeping in general. I would not call the redefinition of the second a reason to delay.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B003 first at opening but moved to B015 because the original idea, experiment and people are clearly identifiable, whereas the B003 credit list is much less certain.
responses.response: This is the argument that gives me most pause, because you know the materials community and reached it independently. I agree that B003 has the less certain credit, and I said so in my own case against. But I read the uncertainty as arising from an unusually rich history, not from doubt about the science, and I think Kane, Molenkamp and Xue still identifies three decisive contributions: the invariant, the first experiment and the zero-field experiment. I would ask you whether you think a prize that leaves out Mele and Hasan does serious injustice, or only an unavoidable one. If your answer is the former, I would have to take that seriously when I vote.

uncertainties: Whether three names can fairly represent the topological-insulator history without Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, or whether the omission is a serious injustice.
Whether the committee accepts QSH and QAH as one achievement in a single citation or as two separate experiments.
How much the 2016 prize on topological phases limits the room for another topology prize.

Whether my field's closeness to B003 makes me overrate it relative to the clean attribution and broad support for B015. This is not settled for me, and I could vote for B015 if the committee finds the B003 credit unworkable.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I know none of the credited names for B003 as collaborators, students or co-authors. My work in theoretical magnetism and electronic structure is related to the field, which shapes my reading of the evidence but is not a recusal issue. I have no link to Katori or Ye. I note the flags disclosed by Kroll, Johansson and Pearce and see no reason for any of them to prevent participation in the B015 deliberation, but I am not a specialist in their fields.
